01Co-founder · 2025 to now

Amdahl

Two of us started Amdahl around a problem that sounds boring until you watch someone live it: government legal teams sitting on tens of thousands of pages of records with no real way to search them. I own ingestion and retrieval, from parsing whatever format a document shows up in to handing back the exact page an answer came from.

The hard part. The documents aren't consistent. Same form, twelve layouts, half of them scanned crooked. Almost all of the work was normalizing before any of the retrieval was worth doing.

02Personal agent · 2026

Atlas

Atlas is my own coding agent. It runs in the cloud so I can hand it something long, go to class, and find it still working when I get back. The goal was never to replace me typing. It was to stop losing the thread on anything that takes more than one sitting.

The hard part. Context. A task that runs for an hour will blow past any window you give it, so most of the design turned into decisions about what to keep, what to summarize, and what to let go.

Always-on runnerLong-horizon tasks

03Co-founder & backend lead · 2026

Radius

A stablecoin payment platform has to prove a transfer is legitimate before it settles, not after. I owned the compliance engine: wallet risk scoring, cryptographic wallet verification, and Travel Rule automation across more than thirty jurisdictions, behind an API that answers while someone is waiting.

The hard part. Every jurisdiction has its own thresholds and its own idea of what counts as a verified counterparty. Encoding that without the whole thing collapsing into a thousand if-statements took three rewrites.

05Building now · 2026

Auxo

A browser extension and a backend that agree on exactly one thing: a decision contract. Before an action goes through, the extension asks the API whether policy allows it and gets back a structured answer instead of a guess.

The hard part. Keeping two runtimes honest about one schema. The extension and the server have to stay in lockstep, and there is no good way to find out they've drifted except in production.

06PurdueTHINK · 2026

THINKedIn

PurdueTHINK had an alumni list and no way to use it. I built the internal network around it: scraped and cleaned the records, added matching so a member looking for a product role gets pointed at the right alum, and put outreach drafting on top so nobody has to write the first message from scratch.

The hard part. Six and a half thousand records pulled from everywhere means six and a half thousand chances for a duplicate, a dead profile, or a job title from four years ago. The matching is only as good as the cleanup under it.

07Healthcare ML · 2026

GNN Anomaly Detection

Fraud in Medicare and Medicaid data usually doesn't look wrong on any single claim. It looks wrong in the shape of the relationships around it. So I modeled providers, patients, and claims as one graph and trained a network to find the neighborhoods that don't belong.

The hard part. Thirty million records and almost no labels. Recall matters more than precision here, because a missed case costs far more than a flagged one that turns out to be fine.

30M+ records98% recall

08Boiler Quant · 2025

Signal pipeline

Boiler Quant runs on data nobody has cleaned yet. I built the async pipeline that streams and normalizes WebSocket feeds for twenty-plus crypto pairs, then layered RSI, Bollinger Bands, and moving averages on top and backtested the whole thing against real history.

The hard part. Live feeds lie. Gaps, duplicates, and out-of-order ticks will quietly wreck a backtest, and you won't notice until the numbers look suspiciously good.

09Network programming · 2025

Clarity

A social messaging app written from the socket layer up, with no framework doing the hard part for me. Accounts, profiles, friends, blocking, saved conversations, and a server that holds several clients at once without dropping anyone.

The hard part. Concurrency. Two clients writing to the same conversation at the same moment is where all the interesting bugs live, and where most of my JUnit tests ended up pointing.

StockGuessr
